# Wound treatment
1. Restore breathing and stabilize critical condition.
2. Stop major external bleeding - a tourniquet buys time on a limb that will not stop bleeding on its own.
3. Scan the patient. Clicking a part on the analyzer's doll, or a part's name in the wounds list, aims you at that part exactly as the targeting doll and the targeting hotkeys do, so the next dressing goes where you meant it to.
4. Remove damage with treatment matching its type.
5. Scan again: remaining wounds, fractures, and organ damage need separate treatment.
Every wound, every condition chip and every category chip on the analyzer says what it is and what to do about it when you hover it, and opens a step-by-step procedure when you click it. This page is the long version of that.
## Painkillers
Painkillers treat nothing. They buy a patient time and a way to walk to you, and every one of them is still standing on the wound underneath.
[bold]Weak[/bold] - analgesic, ibuprofen, ketorolac. Takes enough pain off to get a downed crewman back on their feet. It can never keep anybody conscious.
[bold]Strong[/bold] - opiate, tramadol, oxycodone. Enough to pull a patient out of unconsciousness when pain was the only thing holding them there, and enough to mask the limp, so they will walk on a broken leg and make it worse. It sedates: whatever is in the blood pulls the sedation meter toward a level and holds it there, and the patient slows down. One ordinary dose stays under 60%; two put the patient on the floor; past 60% they stop breathing properly. That is how an overdose kills. The patient feels it coming: drowsy, then breathing slowing, then barely awake. [bold]Naloxone[/bold] reverses it at once; it wears off before the painkiller does, so a big overdose can need a second pen.
[bold]Stimulants[/bold] - ephedrine, desoxyephedrine, epinephrine. Holds somebody upright however much it hurts, and does nothing else.
[bold]Emergency[/bold] - the stim pen. Thirty seconds up on your feet whatever the pain says, and then the bill: the pain comes back a third worse and you are on the floor for ten seconds.
None of it touches blood, and none of it touches air. A patient who has bled out goes down through any dose you care to give them, which is the point.
The analyzer names the tier and the time left at the top of the wounds tab, with the sedation beside it. The patient feels a dose take hold and feels it wear off. Swallowed, a painkiller takes a few seconds to reach the blood; a pen works at once, and you can use one on yourself while you are down. The [bold]analgesic pen[/bold] is the weak rung, the [bold]opiate pen[/bold] the strong one, dosed to stay under the breathing line if you take one at a time.
## Biological tissue
Every topical treats one kind of injury. Used on a part it cannot help, it refuses and says so - check the analyzer first.
[bold]Bruise packs:[/bold] blunt trauma only. They do not close cuts or punctures and do not stop bleeding.
[bold]Ointment and regenerative mesh:[/bold] burns only - heat, cold, shock and caustic.
[bold]Gauze:[/bold] cuts and punctures, and reduces external bleeding.
[bold]Medicated sutures:[/bold] cuts and punctures, and stop their bleeding. The quickest way to close a cut.
[bold]Sutures:[/bold] the plain kind, in every medical vendor, the standard first aid kit, the brute kit and the medical and EMT belts, and printed at the medical techfab without research. They close cuts and punctures like the medicated kind, half as much a use and more slowly.
[bold]Makeshift sutures:[/bold] a metal rod and a cloth, crafted anywhere, make five. Slower and weaker again, and dirty: the wound they close is contaminated and keeps going bad under the stitches. Clean it with antiseptic afterwards, or close it again properly.
[bold]Tourniquet:[/bold] stops bleeding on one limb entirely while applied, at the cost of that limb's use.
[bold]Makeshift tourniquet:[/bold] any jumpsuit torn into a strap from the crafting menu, a few seconds by hand; hold the one you mean to tear, or it takes the one you are wearing. It stops a limb the same way, takes longer to tie, and one hard hit on that limb knocks it loose and the bleeding starts again. Replace it with a real one when you can.
Removing damage barely closes the wound underneath it, and a bleeding wound never closes that way at all. Expect to finish the job with gauze, sutures or surgery.
[bold]Moderate wound:[/bold] external surgical treatment.
[bold]Severe wound:[/bold] treatment through an open incision.
## Embedded objects
A lodged round or a fragment blocks everything else: while one is in the part, the wound will not close and the bleeding will not stop. Select the part on the targeting doll and use a hemostat on the patient to pull one object out; repeat until the analyzer stops listing them.
Any sharp item - a knife, a scalpel, a glass shard - works as well, but takes longer, hurts, and leaves a fresh cut. Digging one out of your own limb is slower again.
## Arterial bleeding
An arterial bleed is the one bleed a dressing will not fix. Gauze slows it, buying minutes rather than solving anything, and it will not take the wound's severity no matter how much you use. Clotting drugs are no better: tranexamic acid halves it at most.
On an arm, hand, leg or foot, put a tourniquet on first: that stops the flow outright while it is applied, and only then will sutures close the wound underneath. In the torso or the head there is nothing to tie around, so the patient goes straight to the table: the artery repair surgery clamps the vessel and then sutures it.
## Severed tendons
A severed tendon is mechanical damage, not an open wound, and no topical reaches it. Open the limb and run the tendon repair surgery.
## Blunt trauma
A bruise pack is the whole answer for an ordinary bruise and for a crush injury. The three complications a heavy hit leaves behind are not items at all.
A [bold]dislocated joint[/bold] is set by hand. Select the limb on the targeting doll, alt-click the patient and choose [bold]Relocate joint[/bold]. On yourself it takes far longer and hurts twice as much.
A [bold]concussion[/bold] has no treatment. It fades on its own and four times faster while the patient sleeps or lies buckled in a medical bed; painkillers only hide what it hurts.
A [bold]bruised organ[/bold] is separate from the bruising over it. Treat the wound with a bruise pack and read the organ's own condition off the analyzer - the organ surgeries are what restore it.
A crushing blow can also start [bold]internal bleeding[/bold], which no dressing reaches. It shows on the analyzer and comes out on the table.
## Burns
Ointment and regenerative mesh handle ordinary burns, frostbite and the damage a chemical burn has already done. Three things they do not handle:
A [bold]chemical burn[/bold] keeps working while the acid is still on the skin. Rinse the patient - water from any source will do, including a spray bottle or an extinguisher - before you bother treating the damage, or it will come straight back.
[bold]Charred tissue[/bold], left when a burn reaches its critical stage, carries no damage type, so nothing in a medkit reaches it. Open the part, graft it with a skin graft, seal it.
[bold]Frostbite[/bold] numbs what it freezes. The patient will under-report a frozen limb; trust the analyzer.
Skin grafts are in the burn kit and the surgical crate, come out of the medical vendor, and print on a medical lathe.
## Cauterisation
Heat seals bleeding. In a fight that means a laser closes wounds a knife would have left open; deliberately, it means holding something hot against a wound with the [bold]Cauterise wound[/bold] verb. That works on a severed artery when nothing else is to hand, and costs a deep burn and a great deal of pain. Use it when the patient is losing blood faster than they can reach a table.
## Medicine
Healing reagents distribute their effect among damaged biological parts. Damage and wounds remain separate: medicine that removes damage does not necessarily close a wound. Clotting drugs - tranexamic acid, and bicaridine and inaprovaline a little - slow every open bleed and stop the lesser ones without closing the wound, and never take a dressing off.
A ladder of painkillers suppresses pain by increasing amounts: ibuprofen, ketorolac, tramadol, and oxycodone, from mildest to strongest. Cognac, bicaridine, and desoxyephedrine also carry a lesser pain-suppressing effect alongside their other uses.
## Fractures
Bones break from blunt force. A single solid hit can crack one, and repeated blows to the same limb break it far sooner than the first hit alone would have.
A fracture is mended in two steps: a bonesetter reduces it, then bone gel mends it, both through an open incision. Osteogen knits a simple break without surgery, and stasizium knits any of them.
Away from a table, a [bold]splint[/bold] does the first step on its own. Select the broken limb on the targeting doll and use the splint on the patient; on yourself it takes two and a half times as long. The break goes to [bold]set[/bold], which is a quarter of the movement and manipulation penalty, and the analyzer says so. It is not a cure: the bone is still broken, it still needs gel or a bone-knitting reagent, and a fresh hard blow to the same limb undoes the splint. Splints only go around arms, hands, legs and feet; a broken rib or skull is surgical.
Splints are in the brute kit and the medical vendor. An [bold]improvised splint[/bold] - two metal rods and two cloth, crafted anywhere - does the same job more slowly.
## Infection
An open wound that nobody treats becomes infected once it has a reason to: it is open to the air outside a sealed suit, something dirty went into it, or it is dirty by nature (a bite, an open abdomen, a round or shrapnel left inside, dead tissue). Under a sealed hardsuit or EVA suit a clean cut holds, and a minor wound never goes bad from the air alone; a minor bite, a round left in or a dirty tool still can. How fast depends on the wound: a clean cut is the baseline, a bullet hole, a bite or an open stump are far worse, and anything a knife has been dug around in is worse again. The analyzer reports the stage per part.
[bold]Local[/bold] is the wound itself going bad: it hurts, and it keeps reopening faster than a dressing closes it. [bold]Spreading[/bold] has left the wound: the part itself is infected and the infection travels part by part towards the chest; the fever and everything else systemic wait until it gets there (the analyzer's [bold]tissue[/bold] line on each card). [bold]Sepsis[/bold] starts once it reaches the chest or the head; it is systemic, shows on the patient's own alerts, and kills if it is left alone. Its late stage, [bold]septic shock[/bold], puts the patient out; the organ failure that follows is what does the killing.
Prevention is most of the work, and it is cheap. Dressing a wound early cuts its infection rate to a seventh; suturing or cauterising it stops the clock outright, except with a makeshift suture, which is what dirtied it. Antiseptic - ethanol, bleach or spaceacillin applied to the skin, which in practice means sprayed or splashed on the patient; the medical vendor sells an antiseptic spray for it - cleans an open wound and lets a local infection drain away over the next minute. None of that reaches an infection that has already spread.
Once it has, the answer is [bold]spaceacillin[/bold] in the bloodstream. It clears contamination in every wound and every infected part at once and pulls sepsis back; a large dose is poisonous, so treat and stop.
Bottles come out of the medical vendor and the medical supplies crate. Chemistry can also make it from cryptobiolin and inaprovaline in equal parts.
## Necrosis
Tissue dies when the blood stops reaching it. Three ways that happens:
A [bold]tourniquet[/bold] is a ten-minute solution. Get the patient to a table and suture what is under it, or use the [bold]Loosen tourniquet[/bold] verb and accept the bleeding, because the limb will not survive being forgotten. The analyzer flags the part as soon as the clock starts, and the patient feels the limb go cold before the end.
A limb frozen through or burned to charring is already dying, and the clock runs whether or not anyone notices.
A [bold]severed limb[/bold] keeps for five minutes. Put it back after that and it goes back on dead.
Dead tissue is permanent. It does not heal, no reagent or topical reaches it, the limb works badly, and it keeps the patient septic for as long as it is attached. The only treatment is amputation and a replacement part.
## Evisceration
A torso does not come off. Damage past its structural limit has nowhere else to go, so a heavy cut - or a blast - on a torso that is already ruined tears it open instead. The abdomen is laid open, the organs it held are on the deck around the patient, and the wound will not clot, will not close and refuses every topical in the kit.
It is visible through clothing and from across the room, so you will not need the analyzer to find it.
1. [bold]Pack it.[/bold] Gauze slows the bleeding. It will not stop it and it will not close anything.
2. [bold]Keep the blood going in.[/bold] Nothing in the book empties a patient faster.
3. [bold]Gather the organs[/bold] off the floor, or fetch replacements from cloning or a freezer.
4. [bold]Put each one back[/bold] with its own insertion surgery. The belly is already open, so there is no incision to cut and no skin to retract - the organ surgeries are simply there.
5. [bold]Run Close Evisceration.[/bold] A hemostat clamps the torn vessels, then a cautery closes the abdomen. Nothing closes while the vessels are still running, which is why the clamp is first.
6. [bold]Aftercare.[/bold] What is left is an ordinary cut, sutured shut. Clean it with antiseptic and follow up with antibiotics: an open abdomen is the dirtiest wound in the game.
You can close the patient with organs still missing, and sometimes you should - a closed patient who needs a transplant is in far better shape than an open one who does not. Holding something hot against the wound stops the bleeding without closing it, which is the field answer when there is no table.
A chassis tears the same way and is called a [bold]torn chassis[/bold]: the torso plating peels back, the components inside it end up on the deck, and what runs out is hydraulic fluid. Put the components back with their own insertion surgery, then run [bold]Weld Chassis Breach[/bold] - a wrench seats the torn plating and a welder runs the seam. That leaves the ordinary hole in the casing, which a welder closes normally.
## Mechanical repair
An IPC and a cybernetic limb are not treated, they are repaired. No medicine, topical or reagent reaches them at all; what does is a tool, and which tool depends on the finding.
A [bold]dent[/bold] is blunt force on something that does not bruise. A welder takes it out, and so does a plain [bold]wrench[/bold], which needs no fuel and does nothing else.
A [bold]chassis breach[/bold] is the mechanical bleed: coolant and hydraulic fluid running out of a hole. It never clots, so it runs until a welder seals it. A breach opened by a round or by shrapnel keeps the object, and nothing - welder included - closes it until that has been pulled out with a hemostat or tweezers. What leaks is hydraulic fluid, which does not burn, so a lit welder in the puddle is safe. A [bold]hydraulic fluid pack[/bold] puts it back, used on the chassis or loaded into an autodoc; oil is not what a chassis runs on, and neither will use it.
A [bold]short circuit[/bold] locks the frame up for a moment and throws sparks each time it lands. A [bold]cable coil[/bold] repairs it.
[bold]Servo damage[/bold] is the mechanical severed tendon: a cut actuator that leaves the limb slow or lame. Welding the panel shut does nothing for it - it takes a cable coil, because the wiring behind the panel is what has to be replaced.
[bold]Overheating[/bold] is the one injury whose treatment is time. No tool reaches it. The part sheds heat on its own, faster in a cold room or under anything cold, and fastest of all if the patient is hosed down with water or an extinguisher.
A chassis cannot become infected, cannot go septic and cannot become necrotic. A tourniquet on a cybernetic limb is a bleeding control measure and nothing more.
## Death and revival
Damage totals no longer kill anybody with a body. Two things do: the heart stopping, and the brain running out of oxygen behind it.
[bold]Cardiac arrest[/bold] is the heart stopping. The analyzer says CARDIAC ARREST and [bold]pulse: none[/bold], the patient is unconscious, the bleeding drops to a trickle because there is no pressure behind it, and the heartbeat you can hear in your own ears goes flat. It comes from a destroyed or missing heart, from blood under 30%, from a brain that is already out of oxygen, from a pain shock on somebody who has already bled out, and from a big enough electric shock.
An arrested patient [bold]looks dead[/bold], and that is the point. They do not gasp, they do not move, and examining them says they appear to be dead and are not breathing; a hand on the neck finds no pulse. Nothing you can see tells them apart from a corpse. A [bold]medical HUD[/bold] shows a flatline icon over them instead of the crit icon, and a [bold]health analyzer[/bold] gives you the truth. If you are not wearing one, assume every body is worth a shock.
[bold]Brain oxygenation[/bold] is the clock. It drains fastest with the heart stopped - about three minutes from full to empty - more slowly when the patient simply is not breathing, more slowly still on low blood. Below 40% the brain organ itself starts dying, and organ damage does not heal. The analyzer reads out [bold]brain activity[/bold] and, while the clock is running, an estimate of how long is left.
What buys time: [bold]CPR[/bold] holds an arrested brain at the damage line for as long as somebody keeps it up, brings it back up to that line if it had already dropped under, and stands in for breathing; it never restarts a heart and it never revives anybody. [bold]Cold[/bold] halves the drain below 30 C and all but stops it at cryogenic temperatures - a body on the way to a cryopod has far longer than one on a warm floor. [bold]Epinephrine[/bold] and the other stimulants slow it too.
[bold]Defibrillation[/bold] is the way back. It needs a brain in the head and blood above 40%. The chance falls with the oxygenation, so a shock in the first minute almost always takes and a shock after five minutes usually does not - but a failed shock costs nothing except the time, so keep going.
[bold]Brain death[/bold] is when the brain organ reaches zero: the patient is dead, with a body and a ghost like any other death. The way back is the same defibrillator, once the blood is up, and it never refuses a destroyed brain. The patient comes back with [bold]major brain damage[/bold]: blurred sight, slurred and stuttering speech and a grip that lets go, for as long as the brain stays damaged. Open the head and [bold]repair the brain[/bold] to clear it; a repaired brain then carries the trauma for about ten minutes, and the analyzer says so.
Nothing Wolfmed does makes a body permanently unrevivable. [bold]Rot[/bold] is still the one hard stop, so get a corpse cold.
An [bold]IPC[/bold] has none of this. It does not bleed oxygen and it has no clock. Pull its cell or break its micro pump and it [bold]shuts down[/bold] - unconscious, indefinitely, with nothing running out - until the power or the pump is put back. Destroy its positronic core and it is dead. The way back is [bold]core repair[/bold] on the torso - unbolt the housing with a wrench, re-flash the core with a multitool, weld the housing shut - and then the [bold]restart button[/bold]. The button checks what the chassis needs to run: a head, a core, a pump and a charged cell, and it says which is missing. A repaired core carries no trauma; the chassis reads CORE RESTORED for a while.
